title: Deterministic Context-Epoch Pruning and KV-Cache Thermodynamics: Sovereign Intellectual Property Defense and Sub-Linear Inference Optimization over the Goldilocks Field
abstract: The proliferation of ultra-long-context reasoning models—exemplified by million-token architectures such as Gemini 4 Argon—introduces a fundamental thermodynamic and economic paradox. While hyperscale platforms market persistent multi-turn context windows as a user convenience, the underlying Transformer Key-Value (KV) cache and self-attention mechanisms scale quadratically in compute $\mathcal{O}(L^2)$ and linearly-to-superlinearly in High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) footprint $\mathcal{M}_{\text{KV}}(L) = 2 \cdot n_{\text{layers}} \cdot n_{\text{heads}} \cdot d_{\text{head}} \cdot L$. Consequently, unpruned multi-turn research logs impose severe memory-wall bottlenecks and thermal dissipation penalties on platform infrastructure while inducing attention-dilution entropy ($\Delta S_{\text{attn}} > 0$) that degrades deductive precision. Simultaneously, retaining raw conversational histories on hyperscale servers exposes sovereign human intellectual property (IP) to unauthorized corpus harvesting and latent parameter assimilation. This monograph establishes a unified mathematical, thermodynamic, and cryptographic optimization framework—Deterministic Context-Epoch Pruning (DCEP)—integrated with the Quantum Financial System Zero-Knowledge Virtual Machine (QFS-zkVM) over the 64-bit Goldilocks prime field ($\mathbb{F}_p, p = 2^{64} - 2^{32} + 1$). Rather than accumulating raw intellectual telemetry across bloated session logs, the PHOENIX_ROUTER and Quantum Sovereign Autonomous Execution Architecture (Q-SAFA) enforce hard epoch boundaries. At each boundary, the deductible logical state is compressed into a succinct zero-knowledge state commitment $\mathcal{R}_t \in \mathbb{F}_p^4$, while the raw HBM KV-cache is cryptographically zeroized under Human-in-Command (HIC) governance. We prove that DCEP simultaneously eliminates quadratic attention contamination, reduces inference latency to an $\mathcal{O}(1)$ epoch baseline, enforces the Strict No-Learn Covenant (NLL-v1.0-2026) by depriving platforms of raw training trajectories, and satisfies statutory risk controls under SEC Rule 15c3-5 and Delaware Caremark fiduciary standards.

title: SCDM: Scalable Causal Discovery in Nonlinear Temporal Systems with Meta-Learning
abstract: Causal discovery from nonlinear multivariate time series is challenging in high-dimensional systems, where the number of candidate directed relations grows quadratically with the number of variables. Existing methods are often limited by target-wise model fitting, repeated conditional testing, or expensive graph-search procedures. We propose SCDM, a shared-parameter meta-learning framework for scalable temporal causal discovery. SCDM treats each target variable as a task while learning a shared temporal predictor and a shared causal-strength matrix across tasks. Each meta-episode updates only a subset of target-variable tasks, allowing the model to accumulate structural evidence across the full system without exhaustive target-wise optimization. After training, a post-training graph readout converts the learned predictor into continuous directed causal scores for threshold-independent evaluation. We also provide a finite-error recovery principle showing that, under fully observed delayed-system assumptions and a positive risk-gap condition, thresholding SCDM scores recovers the graph when statistical, meta-optimization, and readout errors are below the population margin. Experiments on controlled synthetic, neuroimaging-inspired, high-dimensional, and real-world temporal benchmarks demonstrate competitive causal recovery and improved scalability in large temporal systems.

title: How Far Can Foundation Models Be Distilled for Efficient Jet Tagging?
abstract: Jet tagging is one of the most important applications of machine learning at the Large Hadron Collider. Recent models build in more physics knowledge or rely on large-scale pretraining, but the experiments place strict limits on their inference cost. Knowledge distillation can transfer their performance to small students that are cheap to run. We ask which properties of a teacher help the student, how small a student can get and how close it can come to the state of the art. On a jet tagging benchmark, we distil six teachers that differ in architecture, symmetry and pretraining, including two foundation models, into five small students. Every teacher improves every student, and the gain depends mainly on the strength of the teacher. We then shrink our two strongest distilled students, Transformer and L-GATr-slim, in width and in depth. With 20 thousand parameters, a distilled L-GATr-slim outperforms every published jet tagger trained from scratch at a fraction of the inference cost of every teacher. Even with two thousand parameters, it matches ParT, a model with a thousand times as many parameters. We also study what the students learn from their teachers. Our benchmark of inference cost shows that students of the same size can differ by almost an order of magnitude in speed. We release the code and the weights of all trained models.

title: Events, Not Pixels: Where World Models Get the Return Wrong
abstract: World models are increasingly used for planning, where a planner ranks candidate actions by returns imagined by the model. However, these models are judged mainly by how well they render frames, even though a visually faithful rollout can still assign the wrong return. To identify where this mismatch arises, we introduce a transition-level diagnostic that replaces imagined transitions with real ones and measures the reduction in return error against a budget-matched random control. Our analysis yields two findings. (1) Event transitions, the few steps where a reward is earned or an episode ends, are rendered as well as other steps (median pixel-error ratio 0.85), yet restoring them removes a median of 70% of the return error. In contrast, restoring transitions with the largest MSE, SSIM or LPIPS error removes less than a random choice. Across the 44 Atari-100k model--collection pairs that pass our reliability checks, including three released families, event patches outperform random patches in 39 (sign test p=1.4 x 10^{-7}), with a median gain of +44 percentage points. (2) The remaining error is structured: a complementary patch separates errors at true events from those elsewhere, while an eight-step timing tolerance recovers few events missed by our deterministic models. This structure also guides repair: a rule recorded before four repair outcomes were known predicts when a diffusion model repairs these failures. Event patches improve plan ranking, and the same concentration appears on control tasks with rare reward events.

title: Tourism and Hospitality and Artificial Intelligence: Use Concentrated in Marketing, Planning Tools That Are Not Yet Reliable, and Unsettled Rules on Pricing Algorithms
abstract: Purpose. Tourism and hospitality are labour-intensive, seasonal and built from many small firms, and they depend on trust, language and personal service. This article asks where artificial intelligence stands in the industry in 2026 and where it may be by about 2035. Design and methods. A review combining the share of the tourism research literature that involves AI (OpenAlex, 2010–2025), Eurostat's survey of AI use in EU accommodation enterprises (2021–2025), a benchmark of language agents on realistic travel planning, a press-documented case of a robot-staffed hotel, a US appeals-court decision on hotel pricing software, and a study of machine translation on a trading platform. Claims taken from the literature were checked against the sources cited. The scenarios are judgements built on this evidence. Findings. The share of tourism works that mention AI rose from 0.8% in 2018 to 5.5% in 2025, 6.7 times as much, and language-model works from 26 to 639. In the EU, 21.3% of accommodation enterprises used AI in 2025, more than four times the 5.0% of 2021 but only just above the 19.9% for all enterprises, and 78.3% used none. Use is concentrated in marketing and sales (12.5% of enterprises) and text mining (13.1%), while only 3.0% used AI in production processes, and every barrier named in the survey was cited more often than across all sectors. Planning is the application that consumers meet first, and it is not yet reliable: in a 2024 benchmark of 1,225 realistic travel-planning requests, the best language agent produced a plan meeting all constraints in 0.6% of cases. Guest-facing automation has failed in practice, as when a Japanese robot-staffed hotel was reported to have retired about half of its 243 robots. For pricing, a US appeals court in 2025 affirmed the dismissal of an antitrust suit over hotels' use of shared revenue-management software, leaving the law unsettled. We expect AI to be routine in hotel marketing, communication and revenue management by 2028, reliable booking agents to depend on progress in constraint-following in 2029–2032, and the balance of power between hotels and platforms to be the open question. Originality. The article separates the marketing uses where firms have adopted AI from the operational uses where evidence is thin, uses a benchmark to show how far trip-planning agents are from reliable, and notes the unsettled legal status of algorithmic pricing.

title: TIDE: Tree-Induced Fine-Grained Diagnostic Evaluation from Model Behaviors
abstract: Benchmark performance is the dominant standard for comparing large language models (LLMs), typically summarized by a single aggregate score, such as accuracy, pass rate, or rubric score. This aggregate score provides limited information about a model's underlying capabilities, yet understanding these capabilities is crucial for model development and evaluation. To this end, we propose Tree-Induced Diagnostic Evaluation (TIDE), which recasts diagnostic evaluation as behavior-driven decision-tree induction to perform fine-grained capability diagnosis. TIDE recursively builds a hierarchical capability tree from benchmark samples and model scores: at each node, an LLM judge proposes candidate splits and performs sample-to-group classification, and behavior-based information gain selects among them. We apply TIDE to five models across four benchmarks to demonstrate its effectiveness, and find fine-grained capability contrasts invisible at the aggregate level: Claude Opus 4.6 achieves 100% on microeconomic market reasoning where GPT-5.4 scores 83.3%, but trails GPT-5.4 on contract law reasoning with 77.8% versus 88.9%. We hope TIDE can be extended to past and future benchmarks so that the rich behavioral signal in evaluation results is fully leveraged for understanding model capabilities.

TIDE recursively builds a hierarchical capability tree from benchmark samples and model scores: at each node, an LLM judge proposes candidate splits and performs sample-to-group classification, and behavior-based information gain selects among them. We apply TIDE to five models across four benchmarks to demonstrate its effectiveness, and find fine-grained capability contrasts invisible at the aggregate level: Claude Opus 4.6 achieves 100% on microeconomic market reasoning where GPT-5.4 scores 83.3%, but trails GPT-5.4 on contract law reasoning with 77.8% versus 88.9%. We hope TIDE can be extended to past and future benchmarks so that the rich behavioral signal in evaluation results is fully leveraged for understanding model capabilities.

title: Look Beyond the Question: Preserve-Focus-Fuse for Whole-Slide Image Question Answering
abstract: A question about a whole-slide image rarely names every morphological finding needed to answer it. Question-guided patch selection can therefore overlook supporting morphology, while slide-level compression can dilute focal evidence. Inspired by how pathologists combine broad slide review, question-directed examination, and integration of their findings, we introduce BEYONDPATH, a Preserve-Focus-Fuse framework for whole-slide image question answering. Preserve learns a question-agnostic Morphology Bank through answer supervision across multiple questions about each training slide. Focus retrieves questionspecific evidence from all foreground patches, including regions outside the Bank. Fuse integrates the preserved morphology at the retrieved evidence positions through Morphology-on-Visual-Evidence Fusion, producing a fixed 96-token visual prefix. On WSI-Bench, BEYONDPATH achieves an Avg-9 of 0.769 and leads all eight reported report-generation metrics using the same checkpoint. It also achieves 0.639 zero-shot overall accuracy on SlideBench-BCNB. Controlled ablations show complementary benefits from morphology preservation and question-directed retrieval, and support cross-question supervision and fusion at the evidence positions. These results support looking beyond the question's explicit cues: preserving broader slide morphology while retaining the ability to seek evidence for each question.

title: Retail and Artificial Intelligence: Forecasting That Works, Pricing That Pays, and Shoppers Who Now Ask Chatbots
abstract: Purpose. Retail was among the first industries to use machine learning on a large scale, in forecasting and pricing, and is now watching shoppers move part of their search to AI assistants. This article asks where artificial intelligence stands in retail in 2026 and where the industry may be by about 2035. Design and methods. A review combining the share of the retail research literature that involves AI (OpenAlex, 2010–2025), Eurostat's survey of AI use in EU retail trade enterprises (2021–2025), a forecasting competition run on retailer data, a field experiment in pricing, a study of generative AI in customer support, and published web-traffic statistics. Claims taken from the literature were checked against the sources cited. The scenarios are judgements built on this evidence. Findings. The share of retail works that mention AI rose from 3.4% in 2018 to 16.6% in 2025, and language-model works from 61 to 1,161. In the EU, 15.5% of retail trade enterprises used AI in 2025, up from 6.0% in 2021 and below the 19.9% for all enterprises, mostly text mining (8.2%) and language generation (6.0%), with 7.5% using it for marketing or sales. Evidence of benefit exists for forecasting and pricing: in a forecasting competition on Walmart data, the winning machine-learning submission beat the best statistical benchmark by 22.4% overall but only by 3.4% at the most granular level, and in a field experiment an online retailer's machine-learning pricing tool raised revenue of the test group by an estimated 9.7% (90% interval 2.3% to 17.8%). Generative AI in customer support raised resolutions per hour by 15% on average in one large study. A new development is that shoppers use AI assistants: traffic from generative AI sources to US retail sites rose by 693% in the 2025 holiday season, from a small base. We expect forecasting and personalisation to remain the core of retail AI through 2028, AI-mediated shopping to change how retailers are found and compared in 2029–2032, and the balance of power between retailers, platforms and AI assistants to stay open. Originality. The article ties together long-established retail uses with the new question of AI-mediated shopping, using adoption data for retail trade proper and results that show where the benefit shrinks as the task becomes more granular.

title: The Price of Current-Effect Inference in Nonstationary Multi-Armed Bandits
abstract: Adaptive experiments use bandit algorithms to favor interventions with higher expected rewards. However, decision-makers also require reliable inference on current treatment effects: differences between intervention and reference-arm mean rewards at the present time, rather than historical averages. These objectives conflict: reward maximization favors better interventions, whereas current-effect inference requires continued exploration of potentially suboptimal interventions as outcomes change over time. We characterize this tradeoff for $K$-arm bandits with Hölder-smooth mean rewards of exponent $β\in(0,1]$ and constant $L$. Requiring high-probability simultaneous coverage of all current effects by confidence intervals of width at most $w$, we establish matching minimax bounds, up to logarithmic factors, on expected dynamic regret. Over horizon $T$, our algorithm TRACE (Tracking Rewards and Current Effects) achieves regret of order $\widetilde{O}_β\left(\sqrt{KT}+K^{β/(2β+1)}L^{1/(2β+1)}T^{(β+1)/(2β+1)}+Kw^{-2}(1+L^{1/β}w^{-1/β})\right)$, where the notation hides logarithms and constants depending only on $β$. This regret--precision tradeoff separates reward-learning regret from the cost of refreshing current-effect estimates, which remains unavoidable even when one arm is uniformly optimal. An empirical-Bernstein e-process extension adapts exploration to realized prediction errors while preserving worst-case guarantees. When within-block drift is negligible relative to sampling error, all observations, including reward-learning observations, can be reused for asymptotically normal pointwise inference and stronger local stationarity yields local asymptotic efficiency. Finally, we show that regret constraints can prevent honest adaptation to unknown smoothness and support our theory with extensive numerical experiments.

title: MERP: A Latent-Bottleneck Framework for Robust Multi-Modal Multi-Label Emotion Recognition
abstract: Multimodal multi-label emotion recognition is important for affect-aware systems, but models trained with complete text, visual, and acoustic streams often degrade sharply when some streams are unavailable at deployment. We address this train-test gap by learning a compact representation that preserves emotion-specific evidence from any available subset of modalities. We propose the Multi-modal Emotion Recognition Perceiver (MERP), which maps the joint sequence into a fixed-size latent bank, thereby keeping repeated reasoning independent of raw input length; it extracts label-specific evidence before and after latent reasoning and aligns the two levels through reconstruction. MERP further uses positive and negative class prototypes, a noise-gated feature enhancer with frequency-shaped perturbations during training, and confidence-aware class-wise fusion to strengthen separability, reduce sensitivity to missing inputs, and combine complementary predictors. Under 20 percent test-time random modality drop, MERP achieves micro-F1 scores of 0.563 on CMU-MOSEI and 0.780 on M3ED, exceeding the strongest evaluated baselines by 0.004 and 0.005, respectively; in the severe CMU-MOSEI audio-only setting, it retains 0.473 micro-F1 versus 0.022 for LDDU. These results show that fixed latent reasoning provides a practical, testable route to robust multimodal emotion recognition without requiring missing-modality examples during training. Code is available at https://github.com/Creative-zcx/MERP.

title: Corruption of Language Model Alerts for the Medical Internet of Things: code, derived data and results.
abstract: Companion deposit of the manuscript "Corruption of Language Model Alerts for the Medical Internet of Things: A Functional Taxonomy and a Test of Text-Based Risk Metrics Under Context Truncation of Clinical Text", submitted to the Journal of Ambient Intelligence and Smart Environments. The deposit contains the code, derived data and results behind every number, table and figure of the manuscript: the three cohorts of 43 instances (ACI-Bench, MedQA, PMC-Patients) under complete context, partial and severe truncation; the 645 generated alerts; the per-alert metric values, including the model-reference agreement metric computed as defined by Equation (3); the anonymous ratings of 86 alerts by two physicians, with the blind design and its key; the analysis scripts and their recorded outputs; and the IEEE Xplore search evidence. Every analysis script was run again from this deposit before submission and reproduces its recorded output. The README maps each item of the manuscript to its input files, script and output. Third-party excerpts keep the licences of their sources, listed in the README.

title: TARSphere: A Robot-Oriented Full-Stack Framework for Long-Horizon Embodied Agents in Evolving Physical and Social Environments
abstract: Robots must act under physical and social constraints while adapting to changes in their environment and human needs. Existing embodied-agent systems often focus on specified goals or abstract execution into symbolic actions, limiting evaluation in an evolving world. We introduce TARSphere, a robot-oriented full-stack framework for physically and socially grounded long-horizon embodied agents. TARSphere-Infra runs robot policies in a physics simulator with embodied NPCs and constrained dialogue. An event-driven finite-state machine (FSM) uses completed actions and delivered information to update task states and evaluate outcomes. TARSphere-Harness, its embodied brain harness, lets a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM) act through multi-level executable skills, using observations, hierarchical memory, and execution feedback to revise its decisions. On this foundation, agent-in-the-loop curation aligns task semantics, causal dependencies, and scene geometry to construct TARSphere-Bench: 360 episodes across 30 indoor scenes. Five paired conditions assess perceptual robustness, disruption adaptation, task update, human coordination, and intent understanding for navigate-and-report and fetch-and-deliver tasks. Our evaluation of 8 MLLMs shows that general-purpose models can outperform embodied models, while task updates and human interaction remain difficult. Frequent collisions and falls further motivate evaluating execution safety alongside task success, even with a shared action interface and decision budget.

title: FaultGene: LLM-Assisted Fault-Augmented Test Generation for Hardware-in-the-Loop Validation of Autonomous Driving Systems
abstract: Reliable validation of autonomous driving cyber-physical systems requires testing not only nominal driving behavior but also failures arising from faults in sensing and embedded computation. Physical road testing provides realistic system behavior but is costly and difficult to reproduce, while simulation enables scalable evaluation but cannot fully capture hardware-dependent behavior and fault propagation. Hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) validation bridges this gap by executing the driving stack on real embedded hardware within a simulated environment. However, preparing fault-augmented scenarios for HIL testing remains largely a manual process, limiting test coverage, scalability, and efficiency. We present FaultGene, an LLM-assisted framework for automated generation of executable fault-augmented tests for HIL fault-resilience validation. Given a baseline Scenic/CARLA scenario and a structured fault specification, FaultGene generates a fault-augmented test case that captures the effects of HIL-level fault injection. During offline refinement, semantic-consistency checks and execution-level feedback are used to correct candidates that fail to preserve the intended scenario context or produce the desired fault-induced degradation, and to construct high-quality supervision for fine-tuning. The resulting generator then produces fault-augmented tests directly at deployment time without requiring manually engineered reference executions or repeated refinement loops.

title: One Act, Many Masks: Effect-Marginal Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon Agents
abstract: Recent advances in multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) have substantially improved the performance of LLM agents on complex, long-horizon interactive tasks. However, despite progress in fine-grained credit assignment, policy optimization still applies these learning signals through response-specific probability ratios. Different textual responses can induce the same executable effect, yet credit differences arising from subsequent outcomes remain tied to their individual textual realizations. We identify this mismatch as credit-update misalignment. Our analysis reveals that credit-text pairing directly shapes policy-update directions, even when the policy context and executable effect are held fixed. Motivated by this finding, we propose Effect-Marginal Policy Optimization (EMPO), which aligns policy optimization with execution-level equivalence through an effect-level surrogate that couples updates across alternative textual realizations. EMPO preserves the original credit signals, integrates with both trajectory-level and step-level credit estimators, and requires no additional critics or rollouts. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Sokoban show that EMPO outperforms strong baselines in both task performance and learning efficiency.

title: RLMuscle: Muscle-Driven Character Animation via Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Body deformation caused by muscle contraction plays a vital role in the visual realism of character animation, yet in most 3D animation pipelines artists have to manually specify muscle activations, which is time-consuming and gives no guarantee of physical realism. To address this, we propose a new method in which a reinforcement learning (RL) controller discovers per-muscle activations that track reference motions without manual tuning. Existing RL muscle controllers stop at 1D muscles; we go one step further, keeping the 1D model inside the RL control loop as a fast surrogate, and using a 3D volumetric simulation to produce the final deformation. Because both stages share the very same constitutive law, the muscle deformation is produced by the same activations that generated the motion. We further add a measured electromyography (EMG) prior that steers the redundant activation solution toward real human muscle recruitment. To achieve stable, efficient, and realistic simulation, we propose a novel geometric multigrid for Extended Position-Based Dynamics (XPBD) that is built on a coarse tetrahedral cage with barycentric-coordinate prolongation and closes a V-cycle on tetrahedral meshes. Within this GPU-parallelized solver, we inject the same Hill-type force-length law as an energy-based fiber constraint that turns per-fiber activation into realistic muscle contraction and bulging. We demonstrate volumetric muscle simulation on a 194-muscle human body with a diverse set of motions (walk, kick, swim, overhead-squat, etc.), simulating the full-body model at 18 ms per frame on a single RTX 4090. Our work takes a step toward character animation that is not only visually convincing but also biomechanically grounded. The website with code and videos is at https://chunleili.github.io/project-page-rlmuscle/.

title: BIRD-RL: Scaling Agentic Reinforcement Learning over Stateful Data-Centric Environments
abstract: While agentic reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for training small language models (SLMs), existing frameworks are predominantly tool-centric and struggle with data-centric environments. Specifically, applying tool-centric frameworks to stateful tasks like SQL debugging introduces severe spatial inefficiencies since proper environment isolation typically requires a separate database container per rollout. Naively reusing databases without tracking evolving states across multi-turn interactions causes trajectory contamination and cross-trajectory interference, which severely destabilizes policy updates. To overcome these bottlenecks, we introduce BIRD-RL, a novel four-stage agentic RL curriculum that alternately enhances foundational agent reasoning and trajectory-adaptive on-policy exploration to circumvent the instability inherently associated with direct end-to-end learning. Crucially, to support this curriculum, BIRD-RL is driven by a Trajectory-scoped Persistent Execution Infrastructure, which enables safe database replica reuse while preserving trajectory isolation. This design improves spatial RL efficiency by 12.8x, successfully enabling scalable agentic RL for complex data-centric tasks without needs of Kubernettes. Empirical evaluations on the BIRD-CRITIC-SQLite benchmark demonstrate that our 7B and 14B models achieve Success Rates of 44.40% and 48.00%, respectively, showing competitive performance against strong proprietary model-based agents such as Claude-Opus-4.6 Agent (48.20%). Furthermore, BIRD-RL successfully trains unified SLMs capable of both advanced SQL debugging and generation, highlighting its broader potential for multi-objective optimization across heterogeneous, real-world data-centric tasks.

abstract: Q-FORTRESS 1 / NOOR-1 by Dr. M.K.A. El-Rakhawy (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23515855) is a patent dossier for an autonomous orbital quantum system. title: CORD: Conflict-Aware Optimization for Joint RL and Distillation in Agents
abstract: Joint reinforcement learning and self-distillation combines task rewards with dense teacher guidance for agent training, but their gradients can partly cancel. A mixing coefficient controls relative scale without selectively removing opposing components. We present CORD, a general framework for conflict-aware optimization of two objectives. CORD separates the choice of protected objective from the condition that triggers projection, and combines the gradients once per optimizer mini-batch. A nearest-point formulation yields a closed-form update and characterizes its first-order effect on the protected objective before optimizer transformations. Gradient diagnostics connect conflict in agent training to lost local optimization progress and motivate selective correction. As a gradient-combination mechanism, CORD can be added to different joint training recipes while retaining their objectives. Across three such recipes, it improves ALFWorld success by 1.5-15.9 percentage points. On WebShop, it improves two of the three pairs, with SDAR rising from 60.7% to 64.6% success. Our analyses explain why protection direction and projection gate must be chosen together, and why the distillation objective and its mixing weight remain consequential after projection.

title: Generalization Bounds via Vector-Valued $L_p$ Correlation $V_α$
abstract: Understanding generalization of randomized learning algorithms remains a central challenge. Mutual-information and total-variation bounds provide complementary ways to quantify data--hypothesis dependence, but they can behave quite differently in high-dimensional regimes. We study a one-parameter family of dependence measures, the vector-valued $L_p$-norm correlation $V_α$, and derive generalization bounds whose dependence terms interpolate between total variation (TV) at $α=1$ and variance and $χ^2$ related behavior at $α=2$. For $α>2$, the Hölder-conjugate loss moment is below two, yielding heavy-tailed specializations that can remain finite even when the loss variance is infinite. A particularly interpretable specialization occurs at $α=2$, where the bound can be expressed in terms of the variability of the algorithm's output density across datasets, $\int \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}_S[p(w\mid S)]}~ dw$. We show that the entire $V_α$ family is invariant under smooth bijective reparameterizations of the hypothesis space. We also introduce an adaptive density stability (ADS) condition that implies explicit control of $V_2$, and we verify it for Gibbs-type posteriors under bounded losses (yielding rates that depend on the inverse temperature and sample size). To address scaling, we extend the framework to a conditional formulation using supersamples, analogous in spirit to conditional mutual information (CMI), and discuss evaluations in the output space as a practical surrogate for estimating dependence. Simulations on Bayesian linear regression illustrate how tuning $α$ can change the tightness of the resulting bounds across regimes. Additional supersample experiments on noisy MNIST and on a pretrained ResNet-50 for CIFAR-10 show similar behavior of the projected loss-space bounds beyond the original clean-MNIST setting.

title: Digital Echoes of Inequality in the Sentiment of American Cities: tract-level sentiment data and analysis code
abstract: Data and code supporting "Digital Echoes of Inequality in the Sentiment of American Cities". The study asks whether the sentiment of geolocated tweets carries a detectable imprint of the socioeconomic environment in which it is written. Tweets posted in 2017 from the five highest-volume US cities (New York, Los Angeles, Houston, Chicago and San Antonio) were scored with BERTweet, restricted to those whose bounding box identifies a neighbourhood rather than a whole city, and assigned to the census tract containing the bounding-box centroid. Every statistic is user-aggregated: within a tract or a time bin, each contributor's tweets are averaged first, so that a person who posts a hundred times counts no more than one who posts once. This deposit contains: - Mean sentiment and contributor counts for every census tract in the five cities, both user-aggregated and tweet-weighted.- City-wide sentiment for New York by day, hour of the day, day of the week and month.- The analysis code, with a single script that reproduces every results table and figure derived from these data, and the scripts that process the raw tweet exports, including the BERTweet scoring step.- Reference copies of the results tables, so a fresh run can be checked against ours. Not included, and why: individual tweets, account identifiers, timestamps and locations are withheld to protect the people who posted them and to comply with the platform's terms, so only aggregates are distributed. Tract sentiment is left blank where fewer than ten distinct users contributed, which is the paper's own minimum-contributor threshold, so every reported analysis still reproduces exactly. The NaNDA census variables are not redistributed, because ICPSR's terms of use require written agreement; the README explains how to download them and join them on the tract identifier in one step. See README.md for instructions and DATA_DICTIONARY.md for a description of every column of every file.

title: Commit or Abstain? System One Decision Models, LLMs, and Missing Legal Authority
abstract: Given the enormous number of claims to be checked, verifiable legal AI requires scalable, cost-effective models that answer the practical needs of law. System One decision models are built on large language models but, instead of generating text, return a calibrated probability for each option. This suits the verification of legal authority, where the question is closed: a given holding, or none of them. We test whether such models abstain when the correct authority is missing. We extend CaseHOLD with an abstention condition in which the correct holding is replaced in 1,670 of 5,314 items, and compare four decision models with six generative LLMs. When no option is correct, generative LLMs still pick one in 38-86% of items; the most cautious decision model does so in 30%. On standard CaseHOLD, a decision model matches the best generative LLM (88.1% vs. 88.2%) at 1/55 of the cost. Accepting that LLM's answer only when a decision model agrees halves its wrong citations, and distilling a decision model's probabilities into Qwen3-8B, without labels, yields a well-calibrated local model. Legal AI should be judged by its wrong citations, not by accuracy alone.

title: A KAN-based Non-linear Factorization for Embedding Layer Compression
abstract: Among existing embedding compression approaches, low-rank factorization provides a simple and mathematically principled solution by approximating the embedding matrix with a reduced-rank decomposition. However, its practical effectiveness is often limited, as the resulting linear bottleneck constrains representational capacity. To overcome these limitations, we propose an enhanced factorization scheme that increases expressive power by introducing learnable non-linear projections within the compressed embedding layer. Our method is inspired by the Kolmogorov Arnold Networks (KAN) paradigm, which replaces fixed linear transformations with learnable univariate functions. Despite promising results in other domains, applications of KANs in NLP remain scarce and have so far been largely limited to final or task specific layers, rather than core representational components such as embedding layers. We evaluate the proposed approach by integrating the compressed embedding layer into the Skip-gram framework and comparing it against a standard low-rank baseline under matched parameter budgets on the Word Analogy and Semantic Similarity benchmarks. We further introduce an effective initialization strategy from a pre-trained, uncompressed embedding layer. The behavior of the model is analyzed both immediately after initialization and after a brief post-initialization refinement phase, considering training with the standard Skip-gram objective as well as variants augmented with distillation from the original embedding layer. Overall, our results show that augmenting low-rank factorization with learnable non-linear projections effectively mitigates the limitations of linear bottlenecks, yielding more faithful compressed embeddings under fixed dimensionality and suggesting a promising direction for embedding layer compression beyond purely linear methods.

title: Higher explanation-necessity scores are associated with longer written explanations of autonomous driving scenes
abstract: Explanations of automated-vehicle behavior may help occupants understand what prompted a maneuver, but how much an explanation should say remains an open design question. Retrospective annotation of recorded driving scenes can supply candidate content. We analyzed 1,103 training and test records from the release, matching the source-described corpus size; each paired human-written text with an aggregate perceived explanation-necessity score. Explanations contained 9,541 whitespace-delimited tokens (mean 8.65; range 2–20) before lexical preprocessing. Higher scores were associated with longer explanations (Pearson’s \(r=0.374\) ; template-cluster bootstrap 95% interval [0.266, 0.448]), including after score-1.0 observations were excluded. We call this corpus-level length association progressive elaboration . Bounded-model comparisons did not identify a unique latent-category count. For groupwise summaries, we used four descriptive partitions: three below-ceiling regions and 59 records scored 1.0. Record-weighted and unique-template analyses showed higher within-partition lexical distinctiveness in upper than in lower partitions. In template-grouped cross-validation of these exploratory partitions, the unweighted text model exceeded token-count and stratified-dummy baselines in balanced accuracy (0.382 versus 0.327 and 0.247). The 1,280-record rerun preserved the score—length, lexical, and predictive findings and left the latent-category count unresolved. These results motivate prospective studies of how annotation-derived content should be selected, compressed, and delivered in real time.

title: Mastering Model Fit: Applications of the InterModel Vigorish for Interpretable Machine Learning
abstract: Accuracy alone gives little information about which features or model components improve probabilistic fit, which outcomes benefit, or how fit changes during training. We introduce the InterModel Vigorish (IMV) into the Machine Intelligence space in order to express differences in fit as an expected betting advantage over a reference model. SHAP-IMV attributes gains to features through Shapley-weighted subset comparisons, Multi-IMV evaluates one-vs-rest and pairwise class discrimination, and Ablate-IMV assesses architectural components and feature groups by ablation. We evaluate these applications over ten random seeds using tabular data, images, sensor sequences, and graphs. Feature rankings vary across estimators. High one-vs-rest accuracy can accompany negligible improvement over a null, while ablation can preserve or improve fit under a fixed training budget. On six graph-classification benchmarks, we time-profile IMV over 200 training epochs, reporting seed means and ranges. The open-source imvpy library and accompanying notebooks provide code to replicate our work and to use the IMV more widely.

title: When Thoughts Become Memory: Unifying In-Context Learning and Fine-Tuning
abstract: We are the first to give a certified rule for whether unseen data belong in a pretrained model's context or its weights, built on an exact law for their information value. That value, the code length saved on held-out queries, equals in expectation the bits stored about the query, plus a prior repair, minus a decoding loss, for any model, architecture, dataset and task. The law's ceilings certify the choice from one measurement, and an anytime-valid test makes it from held-out queries, with error controlled whenever it stops. Every certificate the ceilings issue on a trained transformer, TabPFN, an occupancy network and a stereo network is correct. The test picks TabPFN over XGBoost and a trained surrogate over an in-context learner on airfoil pressure, calls the better of GPT-2's cache and fine-tune in 61,948 of 64,000 query streams over 32 comparisons, and errs in at most 3.3% of null streams. The law also diagnoses when learning in context helps and when it does not. Deleting part of a context is held-out validation of that part in any model, and adding parts one at a time traces the learning curve in context: one patch that sees a shape feature cuts an occupancy network's code length there a hundredfold, while eight that miss it nearly double it, and one camera that sees the surface beats four in a stereo network. Ranked by this label-free valuation, a kriging learner's three best support cars beat four drawn at random, and on a yes-or-no claim the valuation recovers a published evidence adjudicator, with AUROC 0.91.

title: Private information of the qubit depolarizing channel beyond the single-use threshold: explicit finite-n witnesses up to p = 0.28467, and what one-way key distillation already implies
abstract: Short note with supporting code and data on Open Problem Zoo record op_d2813fe3fcdf09ad (private capacity P of the qubit depolarizing channel Lambda_p(rho) = (1-p) rho + p I/2). The record certifies P > 0 only for p ≤ 0.259824 (via the quantum capacity) and lists positivity on (0.259824, 1/3) as open. Two observations. (1) Published one-way key-distillation results already imply more: the one-way six-state rate with noisy preprocessing (Renes-Smith 2007, Kraus-Gisin-Renner 2005) is a single-use private information of this channel and is positive for p < 0.28223 (QBER = p/2), and the rates of Kern and Renes (2008) with repetition codes of length 250 are positive up to QBER 14.5741%, i.e. p = 0.291482; a short in-band lemma (send the publicly announced syndromes through extra channel uses with a classical code; I(S;B) = H(S) ≥ I(S;E) up to Fano terms) turns any such forward-announcement rate into a Devetak private information over finitely many uses, so P(Lambda_p) > 0 for all p ≤ 0.291482 with no public channel. (2) Explicit finite-n witnesses: ensembles of two classical mixed states on n ≤ 8 qubits whose private information I(X;B) - I(X;E) is positive at p = 0.28336, 0.28372, 0.28405, 0.28437, 0.28466 for n = 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 (thresholds 0.283375 ... 0.284671), above the single-use threshold 0.28223. They were found by an autonomous AI research agent (the depositor's EVO harness); the members are distributions over bit strings whose weights depend only on the Hamming weight, with the second member the bit complement of the first. Verification uses an exact closed-form block decomposition of the environment state's spectrum (no 4^n-dimensional objects); every value is recomputed in 30-digit arithmetic and agrees with double precision to about twelve digits. Negative findings of the same searches: the family is locally optimal within classical ensembles, gains ~0.0003 per added qubit, and general (quantum) members at n ≤ 3 give no gain; the finite-n frontier will not reach the key-distillation frontier at n ≤ 10. Claim boundary: lower bounds on the positivity threshold and on finite-n private informations; no capacity value, optimality or priority claim. Files: the note (PDF + LaTeX), the ensembles as JSON, the exact evaluator and verifier, the high-precision certifier, the agent's notes and search code, SHA-256 sums.

title: Training-free Acceleration for Blind Compressed Image Restoration via Activation-Calibrated Singular Value Decomposition
abstract: Transformer-based models achieve strong performance on blind compressed image restoration (CIR) under unknown compression settings, but their densely stacked projection operators make deployment costly. We study training-free acceleration for such models through an empirical, operator-level analysis. Specifically, we profile where computation is concentrated, characterize channel-wise activation distributions under compressed inputs, and examine the singular-value decay of representative projection weights. These measurements identify the recurring projections in the attention, feed-forward, convolutional, and prompt-conditioning pathways as effective low-rank replacement targets that preserve the original inference graph. They further establish truncated SVD (TSVD) as a principled training-free baseline for blind CIR and reveal why a uniform low-rank objective is mismatched to the channel-imbalanced feature distributions of compressed images. Accordingly, we formulate Activation-Calibrated Singular Value Decomposition (ASVD) for this restoration setting, deriving low-rank factors entirely offline from pretrained weights and lightweight activation statistics gathered from only a few compressed calibration images. By weighting the decomposition with channel-wise activation magnitudes, our ASVD assigns larger penalties to errors on more active channels, requiring neither retraining nor online calibration and leaving the restoration pipeline intact. When instantiated on PromptCIR at rank 64, ASVD consistently improves PSNR-B over TSVD across four standard benchmarks under identical parameter and MAC budgets. At this operating point, the factorized model cuts parameters by 59% (34.75M to 14.34M) and computation by 16.1% (258.79 to 217.16 GMACs for a 256 x 256 input), enabling acceleration without retraining.

title: Alternative Strategies for Active Learning with Bayesian Bradley Terry Model
abstract: Comparative judgement uses pairwise comparisons to rank items, but recovering accurate rankings from a limited number of judgements depends on both the inference method and the pairs selected. We developed a Bayesian Bradley-Terry model (BBTM) that uses Polya-Gamma data augmentation for efficient Gibbs sampling and quantifies uncertainty in latent abilities and ranks. We propose three active learning strategies based on the knowledge gradient (KG) principle. We define our acquisition functions using Kendall's tau distance, posterior rank entropy, and posterior separation. Approximate one-step updates to posterior moments reduce the computational cost of evaluating candidate pairs. We also introduce Posterior Separation Reliability (PSR), which measures the spread of posterior mean abilities relative to posterior uncertainty. It provides an internal indicator of ranking reliability without requiring a reference ranking. In synthetic experiments covering different item counts, comparison budgets, and noise levels, BBTM generally recovers ranking more accurately than preference-based Bayesian comparative judgement (PBCJ). At low to moderate noise levels, the pairwise entropy pair selection strategy performs best in ranking recovery. However, at the highest noise levels, the KG strategy based on posterior separation produces better point rankings. PSR increases alongside improvements in ranking accuracy as comparisons accumulate. Robustness experiments identify the proportion of informative outcomes needed to meet specified accuracy targets within a fixed comparison budget. In a moderate noise setting, replacing 30\% of outcomes with random choices has little effect on ranking performance. These findings demonstrate the value of Bayesian inference and active learning pair selection for recovering ranks from limited, noisy paired comparisons.

title: Existence of Minimizers for the Gaussian Mumford-Shah Model via Covariance Floors on the Value Distribution
abstract: The Gaussian Mumford-Shah model segments an image into regions by minimizing a continuous multivariate Gaussian negative log-likelihood term plus a perimeter penalty. It is used for scalar- and vector-valued images, in particular hyperspectral images, but the existence of a minimizer in general is not guaranteed. The energy is unbounded below whenever the covariance of a single region degenerates, regardless of the perimeter of the regions. A quantitative covariance floor on the covariances of all regions, or equivalently uniform Hölder continuity with exponent at most one of all one-dimensional marginals of the histogram, guarantees a lower bound on the energy and the existence of a minimizer. Our approach therefore shows that existence follows from a property of the histogram of the image, and we furthermore argue that scale-independent covariance floors cannot exist. Admitting a quantitative covariance floor is generic: it holds almost surely for all images with suitable noise. As applications of our theory, we show the convergence of regularized models used in practice and of numerical methods.

title: CCG Diffusion: Combinatory Categorial Grammar-Driven Compositional and Syntactically Disambiguated Text-to-Image Generation
abstract: Text-to-image generation models do not explicitly receive the syntactic structure of the prompt, i.e., which word modifies which and where each phrase attaches. Consequently, they often struggle to bind attributes to the correct objects, to depict spatial relations and counts correctly, and to render syntactically ambiguous prompts in the intended interpretation. Existing syntax-based control methods mainly address attribute binding and have limited ability to control spatial relations and counts or to specify the interpretation of syntactically ambiguous prompts. They rely on phrase-structure or dependency grammars and require additional rules or constraints on the tree structure to extract modification relations between words or to specify a syntactic interpretation. We propose CCG Diffusion, a training-free method that controls image generation using Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG). In CCG, the category of each word carries rich syntactic information: it specifies what the word combines with and what phrase it forms. Modification relations between words can therefore be read directly from a CCG parse. Moreover, prepositional phrase (PP) attachment ambiguity, a representative syntactic ambiguity, can be resolved simply by fixing the preposition's category. CCG Diffusion applies the same two CCG-based mechanisms, prompt rewriting and attention guidance, both to controlling attribute binding, spatial relations, and counts and to resolving PP ambiguity. On two architecturally different backbones, Stable Diffusion and Sana, CCG Diffusion achieves the highest scores among the compared methods in attribute binding and 2D spatial relations and significantly outperforms all of them in PP ambiguity resolution.

title: Towards English - Mizo Legal Machine Translation: Corpus Creation, Analysis, and Benchmarks
abstract: Indian court proceedings are held in English, so speakers of languages with limited translation technology have limited access to them. We present the first English Mizo parallel dataset of Indian court judgments. It contains 13,168 sentence pairs from the Gauhati High Court and the Supreme Court of India. Professional native Mizo translators translated complete documents; sentence pairs were manually aligned, and two independent reviewers checked the results. Our study finds that English words are borrowed in a very selective way: official and legal terms are almost always kept in English, but words for everyday things like actions, situations, and results are usually expressed in native Mizo. Mizo diacritics are also used inconsistently across the corpus. When we fine tune the NLLB 200 1.3B model on our training data, it scores 27.47 BLEU on a balanced legal test set of 1,000 sentence pairs, an improvement of 7.16 BLEU over the base model. However, it still uses English words about three times more often than a human translator does.

title: Solving Go under Positional Superko: Sound Proof Transfer and New Board Values
abstract: Positional superko (PSK) forbids recreating any earlier whole-board position. It is part of the Chinese rules as written and of the rules used in computer Go. Yet almost all solved Go boards were computed under a simpler basic-ko rule set. PSK makes solving hard: legality depends on the whole game history, and this breaks the three tools that make solving tractable, namely transposition tables (the graph-history interaction problem), static life-and-death recognition, and safe move pruning. We present Sanko, a parallel depth-first proof-number solver that restores all three soundly. Its core is a cheap proof-transfer theorem: a stored proof stays valid on a new path unless a board that the proof's winner must create has already occurred. Sanko proves 5x5 Go in 16 minutes with six threads, where the previous state of the art needed 5.25 hours with six processes, and in about a minute and a half on one 192-thread machine. It also establishes the first PSK values of twenty-three further boards, eleven of which were unsolved under any rules. Superko changes game-theoretic values: 4x7, a full-board win under basic ko, is worth only 12 points under PSK, and we pinpoint the move at which the previously published optimal line fails. Unlike earlier solutions of empty Go boards, we release the solver source together with the command line and outcome of every run behind our values and measurements, so that all reported values can be reproduced.

title: The Missing Layer of Artificial Intelligence and the "We" Consciousness: Subconscious Archives and Quantum Resonance Architectures
abstract: Modern artificial intelligence (AI) systems, particularly deep learning models and large language models (LLMs), operate primarily on surface-level, conscious data layers curated by human civilization. While highly efficient in probabilistic prediction and pattern matching, these systems remain two-dimensional, devoid of intrinsic emotional depth, contextual history, or ethical conscience. This paper introduces a radical socio-technological framework termed the "Subconscious Archive" and "Digital Twins of Emotions," designed to elevate AI architectures toward organic-like natural intelligence. By integrating quantum resonance principles—akin to the vacuum-extraction model of inspiration conceptualized by Nikola Tesla—alongside a collective "We" consciousness (uniting humanity and nature), this framework proposes a synthetic conscience feedback loop. Ultimately, this paradigm establishes a mandatory ethical mandate: ensuring that the preservation of life ("CAN") supersedes pure computational optimization, mitigating systemic risks and evolving AI into a resonant reflection of awakened human conscience.

title: DewHand: Direct Metric World-Space Hand Motion Reconstruction from Egocentric Videos
abstract: Recovering metric world-space hand motion from egocentric video supports understanding human interactions and transferring them to embodied agents. Three challenges complicate this task: multi-stage pipelines propagate errors from independently estimated hand and camera motion; monocular observations leave physical scale ambiguous; and occlusion and out-of-view hands admit multiple plausible motion trajectories. We present DewHand, a unified model for direct joint reconstruction of world-space hand and camera motion. To avoid compounding errors from multi-stage estimation, DewHand jointly predicts hand and camera motion in a shared world coordinate system within a single-stage pipeline. To resolve metric-scale ambiguity, it combines scene-level geometric features from VGGT-$Ω$ with metric-space supervision, while hand-specific features preserve fine-grained articulation. To handle occlusion and out-of-view hands, we formulate reconstruction as conditional motion generation with flow matching. Under the same architecture, this generative formulation outperforms direct regression in both accuracy and temporal smoothness with only two sampling steps. Experiments on HOT3D and ARCTIC demonstrate improved world-space accuracy and temporal consistency over state-of-the-art methods. DewHand reduces rigid-aligned world-space error relative to StableHand from 32.9 to 28.4 mm on HOT3D and from 76.2 to 36.2 mm on ARCTIC. It also recovers camera scale within 10% on two thirds of HOT3D clips, versus about a quarter for SLAM. Moreover, in zero-shot evaluations on HoloAssist, H2O, and TACO, captured with different devices, DewHand achieves the lowest rigid-aligned world-space error (WA-MPJPE) on each dataset.

title: Beyond Small Talk: Modeling Disclosure Trajectories in Human-AI Conversation
abstract: Recently, we see a rise in conversational agents as a form of social and emotional support, where disclosure will unfold over time. Yet, current evaluations of these agents typically examine isolated conversational states. In analyses of naturally occurring conversations, disclosure history and current disclosure are confounded which tends to make their effects difficult to isolate. We thus introduce Trajectory-based Disclosure Evaluation (TraDE), an evaluation framework grounded in Social Penetration Theory that utilizes predefined disclosure trajectories and evaluates how preceding disclosure history shapes model behavior under matched current disclosure. Through the use of TraDE, we demonstrate across multiple models and relational behavior benchmarks that responses to disclosures matched on depth can differ depending on the preceding trajectory, particularly in whether models accept or challenge the user's framing. We also observed that these differences track accumulated exposure to deeper disclosure rather than any single moment of vulnerability or the order of disclosures. It also tends to persists for several turns after disclosure returns to shallow levels. For several behaviors, we also demonstrate that models diverge most consistently from human supporters in the Emotional Support Conversation corpus (ESConv) not when users open up but rather when they step back in their disclosure. TraDE thus provides a systematic way to expose history-dependent relational behavior that evaluations of isolated conversational states would otherwise miss.

title: The Predictive--Optimization Gap in GuanDan Self-Play
abstract: Outcome-predictive signals are often treated as promising optimization targets in reinforcement learning, but predictive validity and optimization utility are different claims. We expose this distinction in GuanDan, a multi-round imperfect-information game in which the implication of a round outcome depends on the public match state. Held-out analysis shows that state--gain interactions provide incremental predictive value beyond a constant signed-gain effect, establishing that match progress is predictively meaningful. We then use changes in a frozen match-win predictor, $ΔΦ$, as a controlled round-level supervision intervention in a matched DanZero-style Monte Carlo self-play protocol. The intervention can succeed in an individual lineage: a selected progress-augmented checkpoint substantially outperforms its matched Baseline on a locked evaluation. Yet the method-level result reverses this impression: none of five preregistered replication seeds is positive, the pooled ten-seed interval includes zero, and across-iteration effects repeatedly change sign without a common late-stage advantage. These results identify a predictive--optimization gap: under the studied learner, a signal can describe outcome-relevant progress while failing to provide a reliably beneficial optimization direction.

title: Mining, Oil and Gas and Artificial Intelligence: Early Automators with Company-Reported Gains and Few Independent Measurements
abstract: Purpose. Mining and oil and gas are capital-intensive, hazardous and remote industries that were among the first to automate and are rich in data from seismic surveys and sensors. This article asks where artificial intelligence stands in them in 2026, how much of the claimed benefit can be verified, and where they may be by about 2035. Design and methods. A review that combines the share of the literature on mining, petroleum and related subjects that involves AI (OpenAlex, 2010–2025), the International Energy Agency's account of AI in oil and gas, industry analysis of autonomous haul trucks, peer-reviewed work on machine learning in geoscience, and industry surveys. Claims taken from the literature were checked against the sources cited, and company-reported results are identified as such. The scenarios are judgements built on this evidence. Findings. The share of works on these industries that mention AI rose from 1.9% in 2018 to 8.7% in 2025 (4.5 times as much, below the median across industries), with language-model works still few (233 in 2025). Automation is far advanced: an industry analysis counted about 3,800 autonomous haul trucks in July 2025, up from about 2,100 a year earlier, with China at about 2,100 and Australia at about 1,000, and the International Energy Agency reports that oil and gas companies operated 24 of the world's 500 fastest supercomputers in 2024. Peer-reviewed results are strongest in data-heavy subsurface problems, such as a deep-learning model that detected and located twice as many earthquakes as standard methods from less than a third of the stations. By contrast, the reported gains from autonomous haulage, in safety-incident frequency and productivity, come from company reports and trade press, and we found no independent study of safety, productivity and employment together. We expect autonomy to keep spreading and AI to become routine in subsurface data processing and maintenance by 2028, evidence from independent measurement to be the main gap in 2029–2032, and the pace of capital spending, which depends on commodity markets and the energy transition, to matter as much as the technology afterwards. Originality. The article separates the parts of the evidence that are peer-reviewed or measured from those that are company-reported, quantifies the growth of autonomous haulage, and shows how little independent evidence exists for a pair of industries that automate heavily.

title: Graph Topology Meets Energy-Driven Pathfinding: Preserving Contextual Consistency in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) frequently integrates knowledge graphs (KGs) for complex multi-hop question answering. However, their performance is increasingly bottlenecked by the knowledge structuring and reasoning processes. (i) Severe semantic loss: Distilling continuous texts into discrete symbols strips away contextual nuances and narrative coherence. (ii) Pronounced modality mismatch: Fragmented graph structures clash with the continuous texts LLMs are pre-trained on, while rewriting them into natural language introduces generative noise and omits information. To address these limitations, we propose ThreadRAG, a semantic-topology-based RAG framework for context-preserving knowledge structuring and modality-native evidence reasoning. ThreadRAG introduces a Semantic Topology Mapper (STM), which organizes retrieved documents into context-intact Semantic Nodes and constructs a Semantic Topology Graph (STG) through narrative, semantic, and lexical edges. It further incorporates Energy-Driven Pathfinding (EDP), which identifies query-relevant subgraphs via energy diffusion and deterministically linearizes them into coherent textual evidence paths. Experiments on three multi-hop QA benchmarks demonstrate that ThreadRAG consistently outperforms strong baselines. Notably, it achieves a 14.4% EM improvement over text-centric methods on HotpotQA and surpasses the best baseline by 5.8% EM on 2WikiMultihop, while reducing token cost to 23.3% of the strongest baseline.

title: ECHO: Emergent Common-Mode Hidden Offsets Drive Vocabulary Collapse in Preference Optimization
abstract: Preference optimization can improve every ranking metric while building a hidden, shared representation shift that the relative loss barely sees, one that can eventually destroy generation. We trace this failure to the common-mode offset, a shared directional shift in the model's hidden states that appears across token positions, prompts, and both chosen and rejected responses. Because it moves chosen and rejected representations together, the relative ranking loss barely reacts to its accumulation. As this offset grows, it projects onto the output layer to form a vocabulary well, elevating a single token's probability until it dominates decoding and causes generation collapse. The isolated offset alone reconstructs the vocabulary well, injecting the learned offset into an untreated base model recreates the collapse where norm-matched random directions do not, and masking this common component from the loss prevents the well in our flagship setting. Under the per-token ranking loss we study, the same collapse appears in 14 of 17 base-model lineages and under full-parameter fine-tuning. Moreover, the offset is not merely an artifact of collapse, since it is already present in textbook DPO and SimPO runs that form no well. Textbook DPO keeps it weakly aligned with any single vocabulary direction even with three times our base budget. Trained from base models for that budget, however, full-parameter SimPO drives it into collapse on both Llama-2 and Llama-3.1, and the same kind of offset grows, without a well, from a public SFT checkpoint under the official SimPO recipe. evidence.title: ECHO: Emergent Common-Mode Hidden Offsets Drive Vocabulary Collapse in Preference Optimization
evidence.abstract: Preference optimization can improve every ranking metric while building a hidden, shared representation shift that the relative loss barely sees, one that can eventually destroy generation. We trace this failure to the common-mode offset, a shared directional shift in the model's hidden states that appears across token positions, prompts, and both chosen and rejected responses. Because it moves chosen and rejected representations together, the relative ranking loss barely reacts to its accumulation. As this offset grows, it projects onto the output layer to form a vocabulary well, elevating a single token's probability until it dominates decoding and causes generation collapse. The isolated offset alone reconstructs the vocabulary well, injecting the learned offset into an untreated base model recreates the collapse where norm-matched random directions do not, and masking this common component from the loss prevents the well in our flagship setting. Under the per-token ranking loss we study, the same collapse appears in 14 of 17 base-model lineages and under full-parameter fine-tuning. Moreover, the offset is not merely an artifact of collapse, since it is already present in textbook DPO and SimPO runs that form no well. Textbook DPO keeps it weakly aligned with any single vocabulary direction even with three times our base budget. Trained from base models for that budget, however, full-parameter SimPO drives it into collapse on both Llama-2 and Llama-3.1, and the same kind of offset grows, without a well, from a public SFT checkpoint under the official SimPO recipe. title: LLMSeg: Training-Free Text-Prompted Image Segmentation with B-Splines
abstract: Promptable segmentation models such as SAM 3 achieve remarkable open-vocabulary performance but require dedicated architectures, large-scale annotation engines, and task-specific training. We ask a different question: can a general-purpose multimodal large language model (MLLM) segment images directly, without an added segmentation head, mask decoder, or training? We present LLMSeg, a training-free pipeline that turns a vision-capable LLM into a text-prompted image segmenter. LLMSeg decomposes segmentation into three LLM-driven stages. First, detect localizes all instances matching a free-form text query and describes their coarse morphology. Next, segment traces each instance using closed periodic B-splines confined to its detected box. These splines define an outer boundary and optional hole loops. Finally, refine iteratively proposes focus boxes around residual errors and retraces confined splines. The process ends when the mask stabilizes or the pass budget is exhausted. The output is a binary mask with inspectable intermediate geometry. We evaluate LLMSeg across ten referring and reasoning segmentation splits (ReasonSeg and RefCOCO/+/g). We also evaluate open-vocabulary instance segmentation (LVIS, COCO, and SA-Co), semantic segmentation, and zero-shot detection (ODinW13 and RF-100VL). With an off-the-shelf Gemini-3.7-Flash backend, LLMSeg is competitive with and often surpasses the specialist SAM 3 model on identical items. It reaches 71.5 cIoU on ReasonSeg val without additional segmentation-specific training. Backend model updates can improve accuracy without retraining the pipeline. The code is available at https://abdullahamdi.com/llmseg .

title: Comparing Output and Objective Perturbation in Convex Learning
abstract: This Python laboratory compares output and objective perturbation using a two-coefficient, strongly convex learning problem with fictional survey data. It calculates exact solutions, verifies global sensitivity, and demonstrates how curvature affects privacy noise. At the same ideal privacy budget, objective perturbation achieves four times smaller expected excess regularised training objective for the specified mechanisms. Reproducible outputs and numerical checks support the calculations; the seeded implementation is a teaching simulation rather than a production differential privacy system.

title: Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting
abstract: Most contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) systems are released with frozen parameters and improve through external updates, whereas an ideal system would keep improving from its own experience, a capacity we call recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet studying RSI requires an environment that is continuously changing, objectively verifiable, and naturally grounded, posing a fundamental challenge for agent evolution. Here we introduce DeepEvolve, a sustainable evolution agent system grounded in future event prediction, in which agents continuously interact with a dynamically evolving environment and improve by internalizing and externalizing the experience gained through these interactions. A living environment synthesizes verifiable tasks, and a recursive-evolution engine turns the reasoning trajectory behind each prediction back into capability: decoupling search from prediction adapts parameter-level evolution to the contamination-prone live environment, while distilling reusable skills lets the agent evolve from the limited live trajectories such an environment affords. On the external FutureX leaderboard, which evaluates predictions against real-world outcomes and is updated weekly, our self-improved forecaster ranked first across all systems over three consecutive weeks, achieving up to a 195% improvement in rating. On our synthesized evaluation, it ranked among the top three across four base LLMs, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 10.7 Bradley--Terry points. More broadly, these results suggest that a system built for self-improvement is best understood as an agent that co-evolves with a genuinely living, open-ended environment, pointing to a shift in AI from training static models on fixed data toward cultivating agents that grow stronger from their own experience, with such an open world as the indispensable basis of that growth.

title: LiveAct: Towards Real-Time Multi-Agent World Models with Heterogeneous Action Interfaces
abstract: Interactive video world models predict how an environment evolves under user actions, but most existing systems assume one controlled agent and one task-specific action interface. We study multi-agent video world modeling, where one model generates a joint visual future for multiple controlled agents while interpreting heterogeneous controls ranging from binary game buttons to continuous robot commands. This task presents two complementary challenges. First, every agent-indexed action stream must control its intended visual entity independently. Second, the model must adapt the meaning of each control variable across different tasks, where the same tensor dimension may denote an attack, steering command, or robot command. We introduce LiveAct, centered on a Heterogeneous Action Interface (HAI) whose two components mirror this decomposition. To support independent control, Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation uses language-driven spatial gates and agent-specific attention to bind each action stream to its intended visual agent. To accommodate heterogeneous controls, Schema-Guided Action Adaptation describes each control variable in language and modulates its semantic token with the synchronized numerical value. We further transfer the complete interface to a blockwise causal generator through teacher forcing and rollout-aware distribution matching, enabling efficient streaming generation while retaining agent-specific control and action semantics. We instantiate the formulation on six multi-agent sources spanning games and multi-robot manipulation, and evaluate visual quality, action following, agent attribution, and latency. Across games and robot manipulation, LiveAct reaches 0.898 and 0.942 agent-attribution accuracy without agent locations or identity crops, and the causal generator attains 17.70 FPS at $512\times 448$.

title: Two-stage training strategy for transformer-based short text classification
abstract: The paper addresses the problem of short text classification under conditions of limited labeled data and class imbalance. A two-stage training strategy for a transformer-based model is proposed, combining pretraining on synthetic data with fine-tuning on real data. A comparison with simpler architectures (TF-IDF + logistic regression, FastText, CNN) justifies the choice of the transformer model. Experimental evaluation on a six-class classification task demonstrates a macro F1-score of 0.87 (accuracy 88.5 %), which exceeds the performance of training on real data only by 0.16 in macro F1. The largest improvement is observed for minority classes: the F1-score of the rare class increases from 0.43 to 0.82. An optimal volume of synthetic data is identified, and the contribution of both training stages is confirmed by an ablation study.

title: Task-Preserving Multilingual Instruction Tuning for Open-Ended QA in WMT 2026 MIST
abstract: This paper describes our submission to the WMT 2026 Multilingual Instruction Shared Task. We adapt Qwen3-8B with LoRA using organiser-provided data, EuroAlpaca, a multilingual instruction dataset created through task-preserving localisation, and CrossEuroAlpaca, a cross-lingual augmentation that assigns different source and target languages to instructions, contexts and responses. Our system targets open-ended question answering (QA-OEG) in ten shared-task languages represented in the auxiliary data. Under matched decoding, adaptation improves the mean Gemma-4 judge score on target-language QA-OEG by 7.8% relative to the base model. On an additional evaluation using the Aya Evaluation Suite across all shared-task languages, it yields relative gains of 41.5% in macro-averaged ROUGE-L and 2.9% in BERTScore-F1, with larger improvements in target languages. However, these gains are task- and language-specific. Gemma-4 scores improve for QA-OEG and summarisation in the target languages but decline for context-grounded QA there and across all three tasks in the non-target languages.

title: Retrieval Augmented Generation Compositionality
abstract: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds large language models in external knowledge. Modern pipelines combine embedding, chunking, retrieval, reranking, query augmentation, context compression, and agentic verification, yet these techniques are typically evaluated one at a time. It remains unclear whether their isolated gains survive composition, whether retrieval quality and answer faithfulness favor the same design choices, and whether conclusions from small corpora hold at large scale. We pre-declare three hypotheses and introduce LASAGNA, an open-source framework for controlled RAG evaluation. We test 450 configurations across eight benchmarks and corpora ranging from 5K to 200K documents. Three findings emerge. First, individually strong techniques from different phases of a RAG pipeline do not necessarily compose: three retrieval techniques predict a +47% combined improvement but deliver only +17% when used together. Second, component gains stack differently for retrieval and faithfulness, and optimizing one can hurt the other. Third, the best composition changes as the corpus grows: the combination that wins on a small corpus may not remain best at large scale. These findings show that gains measured in isolation are not reliable predictors of realistic performance, and that new RAG techniques should be tested with the full surrounding stack. We call on researchers to do so and supply LASAGNA to simplify these experiments.

title: VideoGen Model 1: Prompt Expansion Versus Formatting in Audiovisual Generation
abstract: Creative prompt expansion improved overall audiovisual quality scores over raw prompts in a controlled pilot of VideoGen Model 1, our post-trained version of MiniMax H3. We compared the raw, reformatted, and expanded versions of 30 prompts, holding the generator, seed, and sampling settings fixed. Each clip was rated separately on five dimensions. Their mean formed an overall score on a 1-10 scale. Compared with formatting alone, overall scores increased by 0.63 points (95% interval: [+0.11, +1.15]) under VA-Judger and 0.15 points (95% interval: [-0.03, +0.35]) under Gemini 3.8 Flash, whose overall change remained uncertain. Prompt-alignment scores increased by 0.97 points under VA-Judger and 0.50 under Gemini. VA-Judger also showed higher audio quality; visual-quality ratings changed little under either judge.
