Our results indicate that recursive self-improvement raises significant safety concerns, and that strong safety effort should be in place before models are trusted with greater responsibility of training their successors.

title: Ask to Distill: Learning to Synthesize Data for On-Policy Distillation
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) can succeed with surprisingly few training questions, motivating a view of questions as carriers of distributional knowledge transfer. How can we assess whether a newly generated question is valuable for distillation, and learn to generate better questions---without access to its correct answer? We introduce Ask-to-Distill (\method), a framework that treats synthetic questions as distribution elicitors and optimizes the teacher supervision they expose along student-generated trajectories. A student-initialized synthesizer is optimized using a distributional surrogate for question value, computed from a frozen student--teacher pair without reference answers, correctness rewards, or per-candidate student updates. The reward combines teacher--student disagreement with teacher probability mass on the student's candidate support, together with length and diversity controls. The generated questions are filtered and deduplicated into a prompt-only bank for standard OPD. Across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and agentic tasks, our method improves average performance and teacher-gap recovery over unoptimized student-generated prompts and KL-filtered real questions, while matching or exceeding real-bank OPD in the evaluated settings. Signal analyses further show that optimized questions can elicit denser supervision and more total signal from shorter student responses, supporting elicited distributional supervision as an objective for synthetic distillation data. Our code, data and models are publicly available at https://github.com/GasolSun36/Ask_to_Distill.

title: Parano1d: Transparent Proof-Carrying State over Binary Tower Fields
abstract: Parano1d is a transparent recursive proof system deployed on a public proof-of-work mainnet. This paper formalizes its authenticated composition over binary tower fields: specialized hash reductions and heterogeneous parent verifiers refer to the same committed proof state. The verifier binds exact trace slices, derives their terminal opening claims, and closes all claims in one BaseFold/FRI-Binius proof. Nine hash regions of unequal widths share one 66-layer GKR walk. An affine high-coordinate gate preserves each Boolean sum and individual degree while state processing follows the sum of native region sizes. A finite class bank authenticates different matrices and commitment geometries. Each step folds the selected parent's deferred matrix claim into its class lane and preserves every other lane. Terminal decision checks the fresh tip and all live lanes. We prove the embedding identities, public-coin walk and matrix-fold reduction bounds, the bank invariant and finite local knowledge soundness, then reduce invalid state acceptance to extraction, representation or typed-binding failure. The quantitative QROM corollary assumes an explicit database-wide compiler contract. Concrete fixed-hash resource conclusions additionally retain their instantiation and response-price conditions. We report numerical security calculations and complete recursive proving measurements for a fixed reference profile, together with a component comparison with independent and physically padded walks.

title: Exploring Temporal Context-Aware Physical Grounding in Latent World Models
abstract: Learning latent dynamics is fundamental to building action-conditioned world models for planning. Among existing families, Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) offer a natural framework by modeling transitions directly in latent space rather than at the pixel level. However, two issues remain in JEPA-based world models: (i) physical grounding lacks explicit aggregation of temporal context and (ii) action planning always overly relies on generic sampling distributions. To this end, we propose $\mathcal{G}$-JEPA, which incorporates temporal context into physical grounding for latent world models and couples the learned models with prior-guided action planning. Specifically, during learning, we incorporate a shared causal temporal module that aggregates temporal context within observation and prediction sequences under physical state supervision, grounding both in task-relevant physical states. When planning, we further introduce action inference through stepwise conditioning of a generative action distribution on the current and goal latent representations together with their evolving discrepancy, yielding anchored proposals that guide model-based online refinement. Together, physical state supervision guides temporal representation learning, while the action prior guides search through the learned world model. Experiments demonstrate improved planning performance on manipulation tasks, including tasks with increasing temporal separation between initial and goal observations. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/myl11045/G-JEPA.

title: CILA: Confusion-based Instance-wise Logit Adjustment for Long-Tailed Recognition
abstract: Real-world datasets are inherently class-imbalanced, leading models to favor majority classes and struggle with minority ones. Existing logit adjustment methods address this by modifying logits based on class frequencies, but their class-wise adjustments ignore instance-wise confusion and often suppress informative signals from confusing non-target classes. This results in insufficient learning of such classes, increased prediction uncertainty, and limited generalization. To address this, we propose two complementary methods. First, \textbf{Confusion-based Instance-wise Logit Adjustment (CILA)} adaptively adjusts logits based on instance-wise confusion between the target and non-target classes, restoring informative gradients that class-wise adjustment suppresses. Second, \textbf{Batch-adaptation Noise-Injection (BNI)} perturbs the target logit during training, extending the confusion-aware update to correctly classified but near-boundary samples that the penalty alone cannot reach. CILA is a loss-agnostic plug-in module that can be seamlessly integrated into existing long-tailed learning methods, and consistently improves performance across multiple benchmarks. Our code will be available at https://github.com/maya0395/CILA.

title: Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents
abstract: Long-horizon terminal agents may solve a task in one run yet fail across repeated runs. Stochastic errors can propagate through actions and context, creating a gap between capability and reliable execution. We present RiseHarness, a framework for iteratively improving agent harnesses with model weights fixed. It focuses on flipping tasks with both successful and failed runs under the same configuration, using successful runs as references for failure analysis. RiseHarness combines agent trajectories with internal harness traces from a runtime monitor to examine how model actions interact with command execution, feedback, context management, and completion decisions. A Harness Handbook links this evidence to harness behaviors and source code, helping identify recurring problems in mechanisms shared across tasks. RiseHarness then searches other harness frameworks for relevant implementations and adapts them as design references to the current model and execution protocol. Candidate changes undergo behavioral checks and repeated task evaluation; versions with measured gains seed the next iteration. This loop integrates suitable mechanisms from different frameworks into a single harness and uses new execution evidence to guide further changes. We evaluate task success and reliability across models, ablate harness execution evidence and external research, and test transfer to unseen benchmarks with the same model. RiseHarness treats a specific model as the unit of harness adaptation, studying how changes to shared interaction mechanisms can make existing capabilities more reliable across tasks.

title: Claims of emergence in AI should be grounded in information decomposition
abstract: When a language model develops capabilities not traceable to its individual components, when a multi-agent AI system outperforms each agent on its own, or when a human-AI pair succeeds where either fails in isolation, AI researchers describe it as a case of ``synergy'' or ``emergence''. However, these are usually informal assessments not supported by a theoretical framework, making these claims impossible to compare or even meaningfully dispute. Here we argue that \emph{information decomposition can serve as a unifying formal framework to operationalize assessments about synergy in AI systems}. Information decomposition provides a way to distinguish qualitatively different \emph{types} of information, including unique information available from individual components, redundant information shared across multiple components, and synergistic information accessible only from parts taken together. This gives claims of emergence a precise, falsifiable criterion: a system's behavior is emergent only if it carries synergistic information about task-relevant outcomes. We apply this lens to attention heads, autonomous agents, and human-AI teams, showing how it organizes existing knowledge across scales and substrates, while also generating cross-level conjectures that siloed fields would miss.

title: Anytime-Valid Runtime Monitoring of Learned Barrier Certificates
abstract: Learned barrier certificates provide a principled mechanism for establishing safety of stochastic systems, but their validity may deteriorate during deployment when the underlying dynamics differ from those used for training. We propose an anytime-valid runtime monitor that audits a learned barrier certificate using observed closed-loop trajectories. The monitor is intended to detect loss of statistical support for the deployed barrier condition; it does not by itself guarantee detection before unsafe entry or safety of a subsequent intervention. Specifically, the conditional barrier-drift condition is formulated as an episode-wise sequential hypothesis test, and observed barrier increments are transformed into a nonnegative test supermartingale, yielding finite-sample false-alarm control under arbitrary stopping times. Inspired by finite-horizon safety verification, we further introduce a deterministic temporal shaping of the monitoring boundary, making the monitor more conservative early in a prescribed deployment horizon while preserving anytime-validity. The monitor is designed to detect statistical evidence that the safety certificate is no longer consistent with the observed dynamics, rather than to predict unsafe entry. To assess the monitor empirically, we evaluate empirical alarm behavior under valid and invalid certificates. Code and data are available at https://github.com/FormalCert-AI/runtime-barrier-monitor.

title: VibeTraining-Bench: Data-Trainer-Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement
abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires agents to diagnose system bottlenecks and coordinate improvements across training and inference. We refer to the agents' capability to jointly optimize training data, the trainer, and the inference harness as cross-component co-design. We introduce VibeTraining-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating this capability across tasks spanning terminal operation, software engineering, multi-turn tool use, and mathematical reasoning. Within each task, research agents start from an identical initial agent system under a fixed resource budget. Guided by validation feedback, they iteratively refine data, trainers, and inference harnesses, then select and submit a final agent system for evaluation on the test set. To prevent reward hacking, we enforce three safeguards: test data isolation, separate research and grading containers, and network restrictions for research agents. Our evaluation results show that frontier research agents substantially improve target agent systems. For example, on SWE-bench Verified, GPT-6-Astra raises the target agent system's performance from 32.9% to 53.7%, comparable to the human-developed instruct model's 55.4%. However, there is still room to improve their ability to co-design and iteratively refine data, trainer, and harness to achieve cumulative performance gains. We hope that VibeTraining-Bench will serve as a unified platform for advancing RSI, deepening our understanding of cross-component optimization for agent systems. Code and data are available at https://github.com/D2I-ai/VibeTraining-Bench.

title: Fathom SEC Market Ontology v1.0.0: KGSWC 2026 Demonstration Artifact
abstract: Fathom: SEC Market Ontology Demonstration Artifact (KGSWC 2026) Fathom is an experimental, provenance-aware relational workspace for investigating complex information through interactive graph representations, analytical perspectives, and traceable supporting evidence. This release provides a self-contained, offline research demonstrator accompanying the KGSWC 2026 workshop paper Fathom: Toward a Provenance-Aware Relational Workspace for Human–AI Investigation. Included research artifact The demonstrator contains a fixed SEC Market Ontology collection comprising: 2,504 nodes and 8,397 relationships 82 explanatory cards 137 source records Three analytical lenses: Competitive Position, Dependency and Risk, and Strategic Activity The Godot-based client supports interactive 2D and 3D graph exploration, relationship filtering, evidence inspection, explanatory cards, and examination of supporting relationships for derived claims. The archive includes the application source, frozen collection, validation scripts, documentation, provenance addendum, and evidence qualifications. Validation and reproducibility The collection distinguishes direct SEC-reporting and structural relationships, deterministic calculations, financial comparisons, normalized narrative observations, mechanical source links, and derived ontology relationships. The included validation suite checks structural consistency, source and relationship references, epistemic classifications, and selected investigative behaviors. These checks establish properties of the released artifact; they do not independently verify the semantic accuracy of all relationships. Two contextual claim identifiers associated with a derived competition relationship are documented separately in the provenance addendum. Additional source-context limitations are described in the included evidence qualification materials. This release supports reproduction of the frozen-collection checks and offline viewer behavior. It does not include the original SEC acquisition and collection-construction pipeline. Requirements Godot 4.4.1 and a compatible graphics environment are required to run the viewer. Python 3.10 or later is required for the validation scripts. Licensing Original software and validation code are released under the MIT License. Original documentation and ontology annotations are released under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). Company-authored SEC filing excerpts and other third-party materials are excluded from these license grants. See the included rights and attribution notices for details.

title: CLOSER: Evidence-Aware Active Visual Verification for Embodied Object-Goal Navigation
abstract: Object-goal navigation (ObjectNav) requires an embodied agent to find an instance of a specified category in an unseen environment and stop near it. The agent typically relies on an object detector but must judge online from a limited egocentric video stream, sometimes a single frame, whether a detected candidate is the target. Detectors often confidently mistake similar objects, such as a sofa for a bed, and stopping at a false positive fails the episode. Prevailing systems also approach candidates greedily, leaving them occluded or partially observed. We present CLOSER, an evidence-aware active verification framework that treats stopping as closed-loop evidence acquisition, coupling vision-language model (VLM) verification with active perception. CLOSER fine-tunes an open-source VLM to label each view of a candidate tracked across frames as target, non-target, or uncertain, selects complementary views with an embedding-based diversity gate, and fuses their per-view probabilities with a lightweight network. If the fused judgment remains uncertain, a diffusion policy drives the agent toward the candidate using only the tracked mask and depth until the decision becomes decisive. CLOSER runs locally and plugs into existing ObjectNav systems without retraining them. On Gibson and Habitat-Matterport 3D, it raises average success rate by 3.6 points and success weighted by path length by 2.0 points, showing that verifying evidence before committing improves embodied navigation.

title: World2HOSI: A Multi-Expert Harness for Long-Horizon Human-Object-Scene Interaction Generation
abstract: Long-horizon human-object-scene interaction (HOSI) is central to embodied AI, animation, and game development. Existing human-object interaction (HOI) and human-scene interaction (HSI) models excel in their respective domains, but none alone covers tasks requiring multiple interaction skills. Training unified HOSI models is hindered by scarce and costly data. We introduce World2HOSI, a multi-expert orchestration harness that generates continuous HOSI data from 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes and natural language instructions. Our key insight is that long-horizon HOSI hinges not on a stronger single model but on orchestration. Given a shared, structured scene state and an orchestration harness grounded in it, existing experts can jointly accomplish tasks beyond the reach of any of them alone. World2HOSI realizes this insight as a closed loop around a persistent scene state built from decoupled background and object assets. A harness plans action stages over this state, invokes experts via their native conditioning interfaces, and writes each action's effects back, so that every invocation is grounded in the evolving world. To reduce physical artifacts, bounded residual optimization and contact-driven physics simulation further ensure the physical plausibility of human motion and object manipulation, respectively, while preserving interaction intent. Experiments and a perceptual user study show that World2HOSI achieves the best task completion and interaction quality on the evaluated HOSI tasks, while generating more diverse data.

title: Truncate or Not? A Scaling Study of Looped Transformers with Truncated Backpropagation
abstract: Looped transformers reuse a shared block of layers to increase computational depth without increasing the number of trainable parameters. They are trained with backpropagation through time (BPTT). To save training compute, BPTT is often truncated to the last few loops, but truncation yields biased gradients that may weaken the benefit of looping. In this work, we study the value of truncation in looped transformer training in a systematic way: we jointly vary model size, training tokens, and forward and backward loop counts across nearly 600 training runs and fit a unified scaling law that captures the effects of looping and truncation through effective parameters. Despite the training-compute savings of truncation, our fitted law favors full BPTT when forward and backward loop counts are jointly optimized. In matched-compute runs, full BPTT through fewer loops consistently outperforms truncated settings of the same compute. The law further shows that at fixed model size, the compute-optimal loop count and training-token budget both grow with compute. When model size is also free, the law identifies two fully trained loops as the best looped setting. Experimentally, this setting achieves lower validation loss than the compute-optimal non-looped model with about 27% fewer non-embedding parameters and only 8% more training compute.

Experimentally, this setting achieves lower validation loss than the compute-optimal non-looped model with about 27% fewer non-embedding parameters and only 8% more training compute.

title: Optimism Needs a Way Back: What Value an Agent Should Give a State It Did Not Know Existed, Why Every Located Guarantee Borrows Its Answer From a Reset, a Data Horizon or a Reference, and What That Leaves for Unknown Unknowns
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research A learning agent that reaches a state outside everything it has represented must give that state a value before it can act again, and the reinforcement learning literature offers three answers. Optimism values the unknown high so that the agent goes to look; pessimism values it low so that the agent stays where its knowledge holds; a 2025 proposal for agents with growing awareness values it at the average of what the agent already knows, on the grounds that nothing is known about it. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that none of the three rules is justified by the agent's ignorance, and that each located guarantee borrows its justification from something outside the rule. The located efficiency results for optimism assume the agent can always get back, through episodic resets or a communicating environment; where some states cannot be reached, optimistic algorithms incur linear regret, and where some states cannot be left, a 2020 result shows that any agent guaranteed to be asymptotically optimal is, under a stated condition on the environment, destroyed or incapacitated with probability one. Pessimism's minimax guarantees assume data collection has ended; when learning resumes, a value floor set too low makes a pessimistic agent discard a good initial policy, and on one benchmark suite a calibrated floor cut average cumulative regret from 0.41 to 0.22. The averaging rule's regret bound holds under an explicit assumption that unknown states are worth no more than the known average, plus resets. The paper consolidates these results in two tables and a figure, states the choice as a decision procedure whose first step is detecting that a state is new at all, and names the comparisons that would settle what an agent without resets, mentor or ceiling should assume.

title: How Language Models Organize Task Information
abstract: Dense linear probes assess task readability from language model (LM) representations, but do not directly reveal how many features suffice for prediction. We measure readout sparsity with \(k^*\), the smallest feature count found by a fixed search protocol that recovers 95% of dense-probe AUROC above chance. We evaluate 19 LMs from five labs on 14 core tasks. Ten base models give the nine reliably readable tasks similar feature counts and nearly the same order. This agreement extends to the selected features themselves, which on three tasks show cross-model response correspondence beyond class-mean differences and a label-correlation-matched null. Instruction-tuned deployment selectively reduces \(k^*\), with both weights and input format contributing. In controlled synthetic experiments across 20 models, successfully learned targets admit single-feature readouts, whereas readable controls require tens of features. Reference-model \(k^*\) is associated with label requirements across eight students, following an empirical scaling of \(N^*\propto(k^*)^{0.65}\). After continual learning, saved heads can fail while linear readability remains high, and recovery requires fewer labels than initial task learning under the tested procedures. Pruning reduces linear readability, with wider pre-pruning readouts generally associated with larger losses. These findings distinguish task readability from readout sparsity and establish their complementary value for predicting learning requirements and diagnosing LM changes.

title: When Does Better Acceptance Pay? A Controlled Study of Speculative Decoding
abstract: The throughput gains of speculative decoding depend on the trade-off between acceptance length and execution latency. We ask when additional acceptance is worth the cost of obtaining it. We establish a comparison protocol spanning training, inference, and evaluation, remeasuring released checkpoints and retraining six drafter recipes on shared target-generated data across ten benchmarks and two target models. Alignment changes the picture: gaps that appear large in published comparisons shrink substantially under shared training and inference conditions. This narrowing motivates two deeper questions: how is acceptance improved at different costs, and when do these gains improve throughput? We find that acceptance can be improved through nearly free objective and context changes or more expensive token-to-token conditioning. DCore illustrates the former route as a strong baseline with little additional measured drafting overhead. The payoff is conditional: task uncertainty and serving conditions affect acceptance returns, execution costs, and the preferred drafter and budget. These findings inform future drafter design and deployment choices.

title: Beyond Trajectory Statistics: Community-Consistent Human Mobility Generation via Evolving User-Location Graphs
abstract: Human mobility data are fundamental to Web-based location services and broader urban applications, and mobility generation provides synthetic trajectories when real data are costly or inaccessible. Although recent mobility generators have incorporated collective mobility patterns, they primarily focus on individual trajectories and aggregate population dynamics, leaving evolving community structures formed by user-location interactions insufficiently modeled. In this paper, we study community-consistent human mobility generation. To this end, we formulate mobility generation as the generation of dynamic user-location graphs to model community structures and propose MOTION, a Multi-agent framework for cOmmuniTy-consIstent human mObility geNeration. MOTION consists of user agents, location agents, and a global manager agent. MOTION first detects coherent communities from historical mobility using the Leiden algorithm and extracts community-conditioned interaction priors to guide the generation process. Guided by these priors, the user agents plan mobility, search destination candidates, and infer user movements from the individual view. In parallel, selectively activated location agents infer likely user arrivals from the community view. The manager coordinates both views, diagnoses interactions causing deviations, and attributes targeted reflection signals to revise user decisions, location attraction, and source-user selection. Experiments on two real-world datasets show that MOTION outperforms baselines by at least 4.05% across reported metrics of individual trajectories, population and flow distributions, and community and graph structures. Further analyses confirm its robustness, privacy preservation, and downstream utility. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MOTION-04C4.

title: Tracing Recurrent and Emergent Hallucination Patterns in Decomposed Text-to-SQL Generation
abstract: Large language models can achieve strong Text-to-SQL benchmark performance while still producing schema and query-logic errors. Most evaluations characterize such failures only in the final generated query, making it difficult to determine whether a related error was also observed in an earlier, simpler step or appears only at the final stage. We present a drill-down evaluation framework that decomposes Text-to-SQL queries into progressively more complex executable sub-queries and corresponding natural-language questions, allowing rule-based hallucination categories to be examined across a generation path. We distinguish recurrent hallucinations, in which the same rule-based category is observed in an earlier step and again in the final query, from emergent hallucinations, in which the category is observed at the final step without an earlier detection in the same path. Across five LLMs evaluated on an expanded BIRD-mini benchmark, several categories show appreciable recurrence probabilities, while clause abuse shows comparatively higher conditional emergence. Under the conversational-history condition, recurrence probabilities are generally higher and emergence probabilities are generally lower. These observations indicate that the two conditional measures do not move uniformly in the same direction under additional context and motivate trajectory-level analysis in addition to final-output evaluation. Code and evaluation artifacts are available in the project repository. https://github.com/HaydenMM/bird-mini-drilldown

title: HABIT-Bench: Evaluating Habit Induction from Longitudinal Weak Evidence in Agent Memory
abstract: In long-term interactions with large language model (LLM) agents, users reveal habits through their choices and actions. These habits capture implicit user information that agents must infer across conversations. However, individual observations may provide only partial evidence about a habit or when it applies. Retaining past interactions alone does not ensure that agents can infer habits and apply them appropriately. We introduce HABIT-Bench to evaluate how well agent memory systems infer habits from weak evidence and apply them to later requests. We construct synthetic user histories from task-oriented dialogue data and controlled habit graphs. The histories span hundreds of sessions across food, finance, software, and travel. Four-choice tasks assess agents' ability to infer user habits and apply them appropriately. They include temporary exceptions, changes in habits, and suggestions that users have not accepted. Sampled tasks undergo independent human review. We evaluate eight memory methods with Qwen3-235B-A22B and GLM-5.3-Flash. The best-performing memory method achieves 33.61\% macro accuracy across the four domains. Performance remains limited even when annotated evidence is supplied directly. These results expose a persistent gap between access to past interactions and the ability to infer and appropriately use user habits.

title: Deep Learning-Powered Spatial Transcriptomics Analysis to Predict Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Response from Pre-Treatment Digital Pathology Slides
abstract: Response to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) is governed in part by the spatial organization of the tumour microenvironment, yet most deep learning models applied to digital pathology treat tissue regions independently and therefore do not represent the neighbourhood interactions that shape immune activation. This study develops and retrospectively evaluates a Neighborhood-aware Masked Graph Spiking Neural Network (NAMG-SNN) that classifies ICI responders and non-responders from pre-treatment haematoxylin and eosin whole-slide images. Whole-slide images are stain-normalized, tiled and encoded into patch-level embeddings that combine statistical, textural, morphological and deep semantic descriptors. A spatial graph is then constructed over the retained patches and pruned by an adaptive similarity mask that suppresses weak or artefactual neighbourhood edges. The masked graph is propagated through a leaky integrate-and-fire spiking network whose accumulated firing rates form a spatial transcriptomic representation, which is finally classified into responder and non-responder categories. The model was evaluated on an integrated cohort assembled from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), the Panoptic segmentation of nUclei and tissue in Melanoma pathology Challenge (PUMA challenge) and the Phoenix virtual spatial transcriptomics resource, using patient-level splitting. On the integrated test data the framework reached 97.31% accuracy, 96.94% precision, 97.82% recall, 97.38% F1-score and 98.87% area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.947 and Cohen’s kappa of 0.946, exceeding convolutional, transformer and graph baselines trained under identical conditions. Transcriptomic reconstruction reached a Pearson correlation of 0.962, mean absolute error of 0.051, root mean square error of 0.081 and structural similarity index (SSIM) of 0.966. Ablation confirmed that neighbourhood-aware graph construction, adaptive masking and spike-based learning each contributed to performance. These results are retrospective and computational.

title: Push-Pull Attentional Anchoring for Diffusion Concept Erasure
abstract: Rapid advances in diffusion models have raised concerns about privacy, harmful content, and copyright violations. Concept erasure methods aim to address these risks by removing undesirable concepts from pretrained models without full retraining. However, existing approaches often degrade non-target generation quality through heuristic strength scaling (e.g., classifier-free guidance or negative prompt scaling), leading to uncontrolled and excessive semantic drift. To address this, we propose Push-Pull Attentional Anchoring (PPAA), a mechanism in the cross-attention space that displaces target representations while anchoring the scale of erasure via bounded cosine-similarity constraints. By using a relative similarity ratio instead of an absolute difference, our adaptive threshold represents a meaningful percentage of semantic retention, facilitating a single value to be applied uniformly across layers. We conduct extensive experiments across multiple concept categories, including celebrities, artistic styles, nudity, and intellectual property. Our method achieves favorable trade-offs against prior approaches on Stable Diffusion v1.4 and demonstrates its applicability to modern architectures such as FLUX.

title: DuoLM: Fast and Effective Personalized Recommendation with Language Models
abstract: Language models can make personalized recommendations from rich item content, user history, and feedback. However, evaluating many candidates with full-text inputs incurs substantial online computation and limits serving throughput. We introduce DuoLM, a framework for fast and effective personalized recommendation that integrates a compact recommendation model with an efficient serving runtime. An encoder LLM learns compact item representations for offline reuse, while a personalized ranker LLM combines them with user history and feedback for recommendation. We train both models end to end with recommendation supervision and teacher distillation. The runtime further accelerates inference through virtual token IDs for embedding access, shared history computation, and CUDA Graph replay. Benchmark results show that our framework achieves recommendation quality comparable to that of the expert teacher model. On a single H100, it delivers approximately 26,400 candidate scores per second, about 60times the throughput of the teacher served with vLLM and automatic prefix caching.

title: CVCRC-Net: reproducibility archive (code, results, checkpoints)
abstract: Reproducibility archive for the study "CVCRC-Net: A Complex-Valued, Hilbert-Transform-Based Convolutional Network for Colorectal Cancer Histopathology Tissue Classification — A Comparative, Interpretability, and Domain-Shift Study".The study compares CVCRC-Net (complex-valued, Hilbert-input DenseNet) with BaselineCNN, RegularizedCNN and a frozen ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 for eight-class colorectal tissue classification on Kather-5K (64 × 64 grayscale), under one unified protocol with five training seeds (42, 123, 2024, 3407, 9999), with zero-shot external validation on CRC-VAL-HE-7K. All models were trained on one NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU (Google Colab).Files:(1) CVCRC-Net_reproducibility_archive.zip — complete Colab pipeline (notebook with outputs cleared, and the same notebook as run, with all cell outputs), configurations, canonical split indices and labels, run registry and training histories of the 20 canonical runs, per-sample softmax predictions (internal: 20 runs, with and without test-time augmentation; external: all 20 checkpoints, before and after cohort-level grey-level matching), all result files and figures reported in the manuscript, including the additional analyses, and a verified manifest (metadata/MANIFEST.json, 28/28 checks PASS) with SHA-256 checksums of every file.(2) CVCRC-Net_checkpoints_and_processed_data.zip — the 20 trained Keras checkpoints and the preprocessed input arrays. Because of upload limits, this file is provided in seven parts (.part01 to .part07); reassemble them as described in HOW_TO_REASSEMBLE.txt and check the SHA-256 of the reassembled file.(3) RELEASE_SHA256.txt — SHA-256 checksums of the two archives, as cited in the manuscript.The source datasets are not redistributed; download them from their original records (Kather et al. 2016, doi:10.5281/zenodo.53169; Kather et al. 2019, doi:10.5281/zenodo.1214456) and verify their SHA-256 checksums given in the README. title: GPT-6-Astra Understands Touch and Outperform Vision--Tactile--Language--Action Models
abstract: General-purpose multimodal models have shown promise as direct robot action policies, yet whether they grasp the physics underlying real-world interactions and can apply that understanding to guide action remains underexplored. We investigate this question using contact-rich manipulation as a representative testbed, examining tactile understanding as a concrete instance of this broader capability. Contact-rich manipulation requires interpreting tactile feedback and adjusting actions after obstruction. Existing learned tactile policies acquire these capabilities through specialized pretraining and per-task optimization, with substantial data and training costs. We present GPT-as-Tactile-Policy, which summarizes expert demonstrations into task guidance and tactile references for contact assessment and corrective action. GPT-6-Astra combines this context with multimodal observations and interaction history to generate control commands and adjust actions through contact feedback. Without additional robotics-specific pretraining or per-task policy fine-tuning, our method achieves 93.8\% mean success across five UniVTAC tasks. Overall performance is comparable to state-of-the-art policies, with higher success on selected tasks. On Insert Hole, tactile feedback improves success from 31\% to 99\%. Execution analysis further demonstrates contact-guided probing and correction, supporting manipulation progress through explicit expert experience and online feedback.

title: When Does Experience Memory Help Closed-Loop LLM Driving Agents? A Controlled Evaluation with Resampled Warmup Pools, Token-Matched Fillers, and Audited Baselines
abstract: When does experience memory help a closed-loop LLM driving agent? Published gains cannot say, because the two factors we find to matter most, which warmup experiences the pool contains and what any injected tokens do to the prompt, are controlled in none of them. We answer with a controlled evaluation on one audited HighwayEnv testbed (1Hz, gpt-4o-mini for the decisive contrasts). We treat the warmup pool as a resampled random factor (ten disjoint pools) and add token-matched irrelevant-filler controls, oracle-certified diagnostics, caution-pricing metrics, and quantified audits of the baseline ports. The probe suite spans flat-text retrieval (a DiLu port), a single-frame grid port (RESPOND-inspired), our episodic temporal-graph memory, a retrieval-free consolidated rulebook, and a flat K-step observation-history baseline. Four findings follow, each a property of this testbed. (1) Headline memory gains belong to the warmup draw. The reported pool is the best of ten for both retrieval memories, which beat No-Memory in only one pool of ten (sign test p=0.011), and even the rulebook's apparent pool-immunity collapsed on five fresh draws. (2) No retrieval design tested exceeds token-matched filler. The collision-only merge ceiling is reached by a single 15-token caution instruction, and metrics that price caution erase the rulebook's lead. (3) Representational sophistication is nowhere robustly operative. (4) Baseline port quality silently inverts conclusions. evidence.title: When Does Experience Memory Help Closed-Loop LLM Driving Agents? A Controlled Evaluation with Resampled Warmup Pools, Token-Matched Fillers, and Audited Baselines
evidence.abstract: When does experience memory help a closed-loop LLM driving agent? Published gains cannot say, because the two factors we find to matter most, which warmup experiences the pool contains and what any injected tokens do to the prompt, are controlled in none of them. We answer with a controlled evaluation on one audited HighwayEnv testbed (1Hz, gpt-4o-mini for the decisive contrasts). We treat the warmup pool as a resampled random factor (ten disjoint pools) and add token-matched irrelevant-filler controls, oracle-certified diagnostics, caution-pricing metrics, and quantified audits of the baseline ports. The probe suite spans flat-text retrieval (a DiLu port), a single-frame grid port (RESPOND-inspired), our episodic temporal-graph memory, a retrieval-free consolidated rulebook, and a flat K-step observation-history baseline. Four findings follow, each a property of this testbed. (1) Headline memory gains belong to the warmup draw. The reported pool is the best of ten for both retrieval memories, which beat No-Memory in only one pool of ten (sign test p=0.011), and even the rulebook's apparent pool-immunity collapsed on five fresh draws. (2) No retrieval design tested exceeds token-matched filler. The collision-only merge ceiling is reached by a single 15-token caution instruction, and metrics that price caution erase the rulebook's lead. (3) Representational sophistication is nowhere robustly operative. (4) Baseline port quality silently inverts conclusions. On this testbed, a single-pool comparison without filler controls would have reported memory gains that these controls reverse. We release the testbed, audited ports, seeds, and caches.

title: MultiAgent-OPD: End-to-End Training of Hierarchical Multi-Agent Systems with On-Policy Distillation
abstract: In a hierarchical multi-agent system, a Leader assigns tasks and subagents carry them out. Jointly training the Leader and the subagents is difficult because a final answer gives only indirect feedback to the subagents. An LLM judge can score the performance of the subagents, but these scores depend on the judge's own assessment of the quality of subagents' responses. We present MultiAgent-OPD, which combines on-policy distillation with reinforcement learning to jointly train a shared-parameter Leader-Searcher-Answerer team end to end. We first train a Teacher in a Searcher-Answerer workflow using answer correctness. During team training, the frozen Teacher scores student-generated search and summary tokens to provide local process supervision for the Searchers, while the Leader learns from team success and the Answerer from candidate correctness. Across seven datasets, the trained system reaches 38.68% macro avg@4, exceeding Prompted Critic by 4.06 percentage points and C-MAS + RL, the trained cascaded multiagent system, by 2.61 percentage points. The team also solves more questions within four attempts.

title: Stim Circuits and Numerical Data for High-Accuracy Propagation Assisted Local Decoding for Fast Transversal Clifford Circuits
abstract: This dataset contains the Stim circuits and numerical data accompanying the paper High-Accuracy Propagation Assisted Local Decoding for Fast Transversal Clifford Circuits by Mark Webber, Simanraj Sadana, Matthew A. Lane, Lucy Jade Robson, and Anthony O'Rourke. The archive includes: Stim circuits: Quantum circuits used in the numerical simulations, DEM creation, and decoding benchmarks presented in the paper. Numerical data: CSV files containing the results underlying the paper's figures and decoder-performance comparisons. Documentation: A README describing the files, simulation configurations, and their correspondence to the figures in the manuscript. These materials are provided to support reproducibility and independent analysis of the reported results.
